newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Costello moves U.S. market with gaffe.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Costello moves U.S. market with gaffe.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello moved the U.S. bond market with remarks labelled here as an "outrageous" gaffe after he quoted the U.S. Federal Reserve chairman as saying inflation posed no short-term threat.

Costello, who met Alan Greenspan in private in Washington on Monday, found himself the reluctant focus of world markets and media criticism back home on Wednesday after his comments were seen by U.S. bond traders as ruling out a U.S. rate hike.
In what is believed to be the first time an Australian government minister has moved the world's biggest bond market, Costello said Greenspan seemed optimistic on U.S. inflation.

"He (Greenspan) indicated to me that he saw no threats to inflation down the track," Costello told some Australian journalists covering meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in the U.S. capital.

"So he indicated to me that there was no reason to expect a change on the current scene as he sees it. He was very optimistic. He's got a conjunction of strong growth in the U.S., near full employment and the lowest inflation in 30 years," he added.

The remarks took time to filter through to the Treasuries market, eventually finding their way onto the screens of delighted bond traders on Tuesday when they found them in an Australian media report posted on the Internet.
The traders went on a buying spree. The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended 19/32 higher at 98-13/32 on Tuesday, paring the yield back to 6.88 percent from 6.92 percent on Monday.
The Internet report was posted by The Australian Financial Review newspaper, which has a web site on the world-wide computer network and splashed Costello's remarks on its front page here.
But Costello was not keen to take credit for his Australian coup when later cornered by foreign reporters in Washington.
"I don't comment on other countries'...policies," he said when asked by Reuters about the newspaper report. When read portions of the report, Costello said: "That's fanciful."

However, the state-owned Australian Broadcasting Corp later broadcast a tape-recording of Costello's Washington remarks. The opposition Labor party here immediately accused the treasurer of making a "false denial".

"Peter Costello has shown today that he is simply not fit to be Australia's treasurer after the appalling indiscretion that he committed in Washington," opposition treasury spokesman and former foreign minister Gareth Evans said on Wednesday.

"He has embarrassed us in the eyes of the world....How can he ever be trusted again with a confidence by any senior minister or senior bank official after his outrageous breach of faith," Evans told reporters.
Television media also took up the story, with a prime-time current affairs show entitling their report, "Loose Lips".
One market economist in Australia expressed doubt the U.S. monetary-policy chief would even share his views on the stance of current policy with a visiting Australian treasurer.

"It's fairly unusual for Alan Greenspan to share his views about interest rates with anyone, let along a finance minister from another country that he has never met," said Saul Eslake, chief economist with the ANZ Banking Group.
"I'd be very surprised if he went on to tell the Australian treasurer what he has reported to have done about the outlook for U.S. interest rates. Its highly unusual," Eslake added.
Australian politicians, including Evans, have made a string of notable gaffes on their travels abroad in recent years.
